narrative:
The model predicted a 67% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Standing in the bottom decile is far below the average of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaling that your later-year performance raised serious concerns about readiness for the bar.

Your LSAT score of 36 was the second most important factor. Although this score is only slightly below the average of 37.2 among accepted applicants, it still nudged the prediction modestly toward passing. Unfortunately, this small positive effect was not enough to offset the other signals.

Your first-year class ranking came in third. Like your third-year rank, being in the bottom decile—compared with an average around the sixth decile for accepted students—again pulled the outcome toward failure.

Taken together, your consistently low class standing in both early and later years outweighed the near-average LSAT and led the model to conclude that the risk of failing the bar was too high for admission.

What you should do next is focus on improving your academic performance and retaking the LSAT if possible. Raising your class rank and boosting your test score would directly address the factors that hurt your application most. Many students successfully reapply after strengthening these areas.
